utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem is that I can't hear you. Yes, appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's Joanna Korner and Nicholas Koumjian assisted by Denise Gustin case manager this morning. Your Honours, may I wish you all a Happy New Year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I wished you all a Happy New Year before I left and I repeat it and hope it will be a good year for everyone. I started it off really well, becoming a grandpa yesterday. So Mr. Ackerman appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning and Happy New Year, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, and I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic. Nice to see you all again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and Happy New Year to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are I'm afraid a number of matters that have arisen over the break, administratively. Can I say this, Your Honour? I'm very anxious that this morning's witness finishes because he's got to potentially appear, reappear in the Stakic case this afternoon, so I wonder if I could delay discussion of those matters until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, actually, before I even hear Mr. Ackerman, I had a short meeting with one of the senior members of my staff this morning, and I asked him to pass on a message at the right moment to both Defence and Prosecution that it will definitely be the practice that we will be adopting this year that administrative matters, unless they are really important and urgent, will only be dealt with at the end of the sitting, rather than at the beginning. So that we avoid keeping the witnesses waiting sometimes for half an hour, three-quarters of an hour and so on. So unless you have something really urgent or unless Mr. Ackerman has really got asking really urgent to press forward, we will leave the administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in theory that's a wonderful idea except nobody -- and I say this I'm as much to blame as anyone, nobody ever estimates correctly how long anything will take so asking to leave ten minutes -- I think, Your Honour, tomorrow morning, it would be better because they are really matters we need to clear up quite soon. They relate to matters like Rule 92, Your Honour's order, there is a long list of matters but I would ask this morning that we go straight into Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I also have several matters to bring up, but I haven't had time to discuss them with the other two judges in any case so we will bring these up later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honour, I wonder if we could maybe we need to say tomorrow morning that the first hour and we will let the witness who is coming tomorrow and will be here for a couple of days know that he won't be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Provided you don't bring the witness and keep him waiting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That will be fine with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, so let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, Mr. Koumjian is going to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is to make sure because it's 7.179?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no idea. No. It's Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's not a protected witness, so I don't know what the number. Oh, it is .179. Your Honour, one other aspect that I ought to mention just in case, tomorrow's witness who is a fairly major witness was due to arrive last Wednesday. Owing to the weather conditions, he didn't. In fact he didn't get here until Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He is here. He had to go through documents and videos. I don't know whether Your Honour has yet had the list, probably not, but I've compiled the list of the documents and videos for tomorrow over the weekend. I hope, although I have to go into Stakic briefly this afternoon to be able to deal with any matters that arise today, but it may be that I'll have to ask Your Honour in any event for a delay. But I hope not because I'm sincerely anxious as I know Your Honours are to get on with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is necessary, I'm sure there won't be any problems either from the Defence and certainly not from this side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honours be very kind and excuse me for today, therefore?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Korner. Thank you. Usher, could you please -- the witness does not enjoy any protective measures, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he's never given evidence before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't have an indication of the -- I do have the -- all right. Sorry. I was looking at another number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We will proffer his Stakic testimony, but the witness also testified in the Omarska case. But we are only proffering the Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I was looking at another number by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If Your Honour wants, while the witness is being brought in, I could mark the transcript from that trial as Prosecution's next exhibit, which I believe would P1547.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure how the Court has handled exhibits from the Stakic case. We would be at the same time moving to admit all of the exhibits that were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do have them. The thing is that -- anyway, let's move ahead. Good morning to you, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence, and I know that this is not the first time. So I need barely repeat what you have to do. In other words, stand up, take the piece of paper that you will be handed, which contains a solemn declaration to speak the truth, and you kindly proceed by making that solemn declaration. That will be your undertaking with this Chamber that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. You will first be asked a series of questions by Mr. Koumjian who is the Prosecution official officer in this case handling your testimony. After that, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman, who is appearing for the accused in this case, who is Radoslav Brdjanin. Mr. Koumjian, the witness is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could first, perhaps, handle that administrative matters of the prior transcript. We would be moving in the P1547 and all of the exhibits that were part of that testimony, including a videotape. I don't think -- we will play the videotape if Your Honours request it, but I don't think it's necessary as long as it's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not been given to me. So at this point, I oppose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think the objection cannot but be sustained if it hasn't been given to Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just explain the history of that. I'm not sure of the history of the discovery. Ms. Gustin might -- but that particular videotape was not in the hands of the OTP until Mr. Sivac testified last July, and the transcript of Mr. Sivac that was disclosed includes references to the videotape. In fact, it includes a partial transcript of the videotape. The transcript -- the testimony of Mr. Sivac from the Stakic trial does not make complete sense without having that videotape that he refers to for several pages. It was actually disclosed on my understanding from Ms. Gustin on the 29th of October, 2002. So that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps you could check that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not concerned about the videotape. It's the transcript and the exhibits that I'm concerned about. It has become the rule in this Chamber that anything they give to the Trial Chamber has to also be given to me, and it hasn't been given to me. It should be a redacted transcript. I've not seen it, so I don't know if the redactions were properly done, and I don't have the attached exhibits that are being submitted to the Trial Chamber. And that's my objection and I think it's an appropriate objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's postpone this particular issue until after the first break. In the meantime, I suppose that during the first break, you will discuss it amongst yourself and come to sort some of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you are saying one thing and he is saying another, and I need to have a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not questioning him at all, and I do have the redacted transcript to provide him now. Apparently the redacted transcript was not provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And with Your Honour's consent, I'm going to skip over all introductions and all matters referred to that are not redacted from the transcript and simply go to those matters that are were redacted in that perhaps a few matters that could be clarified from the prior transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, you did testify in your -- in the Stakic case regarding your career with the -- under various names, with the police, or the security whatever names are given for those services in Prijedor. You also testified regarding your internment in the Omarska camp until -- and you were not released until the day after the foreign journalists visited. Can you tell the Court, in the Omarska camp, did you see interrogators, persons who were responsible for the questioning of persons interned in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Why, yes. Very often there were my colleagues who used to work with me in the security service. Most of them. They were only a few investigators whom I did not know and I received information from people who went for interrogation -- in for interrogation, that they had come from Banja Luka. The last name of one of them was Popovic. I'm not sure about his first name. I think it is Mane. In my police career, I met that man several times. We sometimes cooperated in same assignments. And another man who came from Banja Luka in a car with Banja Luka plates, and as far as I can remember, he was from the state security service in Banja Luka and the two of them would arrive to Omarska every morning in that car. Other investigators were people I knew well from Prijedor. Most of them were employed by the security service in Prijedor, that is in SUP, Secretariat of the Interior, that is what I will call it. One of them worked for the state security detached office in Prijedor. That particular office in Prijedor is a forward office, is a detached office of the security services centre in Banja Luka. And the terms of reference of that particular office of the state security office in Prijedor were to cover the municipalities of Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, and Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Among the interrogators, did you -- or investigators doing the interrogation, were there persons that you knew, recognised, or learned were military -- members of the military or army?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. There was -- there were no members of the army there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you give us then the categories of the interrogators? You mentioned -- is it correct that there were members of the regular -- of the police. Would that be the crime suppression department, the normal police service in the city of Banja Luka, the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The chief of the interrogators in the camp was Ranko Mijic, and I knew him very well. He was the chief before in 1992, of the criminal investigations service in the Prijedor SUP. Besides him there was also Drago Meakic, who was a retired inspector, and he was actually the uncle of Zeljko Meakic who was the commander of the Omarska camp. There was also Nebojsa Babic there, Neso Tomcic. They were also active interrogators in the Prijedor SUP. There was also Zare Tejic, who was a crime technician, who actually went out on site investigations in the SUP -- Prijedor. Rade Knezevic was a retired interrogator in the Prijedor SUP. Obrad Despotovic, he was in charge of monitoring foreigners on behalf of the SUP, and he monitored them while they were there. There were also work -- people there working who were outside of the security service. One of the roughest interrogators in the Omarska camp was Dragan Radakovic. He was an art teacher. But in 1992, he was performing the duty of the director of the Kozara national park. Boro or Dragan Milosavljevic also worked as a an interrogator in the camp, he was an agronomist. And I know that he worked in the agricultural combine of Agrounija. Another very rough interrogator in the Omarska camp, and I know this because all those who went to have an interview with him, came back with visible signs of violence, and his name was Miroslav Zoric. He was a teacher, a teacher at the school of electronics in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- both answers the witness has given have not been responsive to the questions. They are going off on very long tangents. The questions were quite simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was: Can you give us then the categories of the interrogators. You mentioned, is it correct, that there were members of the regular, of the police. Would that be the crime suppression department? And I lost the line there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me -- perhaps I can try to summarise it a bit better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because, Mr. -- partly you are right and partly he is answering the question and partly he's not. So if you can bring your witness to order, Mr. Koumjian, I think that would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac what I would like you to explain to the Judges is not the individuals' names but the organisations that they belong to. Would it be correct that there were interrogators, as you've already mentioned in your last answer, who were from the crime suppression department, the regular police. You've also told us about there being interrogators from the state security. And would it be correct that these were persons who normally worked in the SUP building in Prijedor but reported to Banja Luka to Stojan Zupljanin in Banja Luka. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony in the Stakic case, you talked on direct and then added some more information on cross-examination about some discussions that you had following your release from Omarska in the Trnopolje camp with Mr. Ecem and, I believe, Mr. Rade Mucic, I'm not sure I'm pronouncing his name, the second individual. Can you tell the Court, first of all, how you know those two individuals.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I've known Rade Mucic and Zivko Ecem a long time before 1992 because they used to work for Kozarski Vjesnik which is the local paper and for the local radio station, Radio Prijedor. Rade Mucic at that time was also a correspondent for a newspaper which came at the RMK, that is the metal works in Zenica, mining and metal works in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And it is in your transcript but to remind the judges, you had a long career in journalism working at the federal level with Sarajevo Television. And is that how you came into contact, into professional contact with these individuals?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Quite often some events which I covered for the -- for Sarajevo Television, Rade Mucic and Zivko Ecem also covered it those events for their respective newspapers or stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So now if you could please tell us, in as much detail as you recall now, about the discussions you had in the Trnopolje camp with Rade Mucic and Zivko Ecem and what they told you about the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: My contacts with them were spontaneous. I did not want to meet them, being aware of all that they had done before. I knew that they were very close with Admiral Zeljaja, commander of the Prijedor Brigade. They were practically his spokesmen, responsible for his public relations. When I -- as I waited in a queue in front of the infirmary in Trnopolje to seek medical help, because in Omarska, my health was severely impaired, all of a sudden, from behind my back, one caught me by my shoulder and said, "Where are you, Sivi? What are you doing here?" It was Rade Mutic. I turned and he said in a tone which was almost compassionate, that he was sort of apologising to me, for having been put in Omarska and there was no help for anyone in Omarska. Only he said in front of me and I suppose he was trying to wash his hands, the only man to whom -- whom he, Rade Mutic and Zivko Ecem helped was Ratim Seferovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could stop you now, can you tell us briefly who was Mr. Seferovic and how would Mr. Ecem and Mutic have known him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Ratim Seferovic was a teacher of literature, and before 1992, he was the director of the Kozarski Vjesnik and Radio Prijedor and they were the same -- also Zivko Ecem and Rade Mutic also worked in that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that they told you that they helped Mr. Seferovic. You said he was the only person that they helped. Did they explain that, that he was the only one that they tried to help or the only one that they could help?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They said that he was the only person that they had helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us in as much detail as you recall now, exactly what they told you about how they were able to help Mr. Seferovic? First I should ask you to clarify, did you see Mr. Seferovic in the Omarska camp? Was he detained with you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. He wasn't detained with me. When I came to Omarska, he was -- he had already left the camp. They said that they had to write Mr. Ratim Seferovic's biography, and they took that to the commander of the 43rd Motorised Brigade, Radmilo Zeljaja, and then Radmilo Zeljaja took that biography to a meeting of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor. And there he managed to reach an accord or to get approval for Ratim Seferovic to be released from the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Now I want to go to a couple of documents that were discussed in the Stakic case, and counsel can tell me if he doesn't have them. And if that's true then, we'll wait until later do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have what was marked in the Stakic case, it's a colour copy, S242/1, it appears to be an issue of Kozarski Vjesnik from the 17th of July, 1992, the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have this document, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, first if that document could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, there appear to be two articles in that -- on that first page. Can you read slowly for the record the headline of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which of the two sheets are you referring the witness to? Because what we have is S242/1 and S242/2. S/1 is this one, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. I handed him S/1, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And we have some parts of it which are highlighted, have they been highlighted for the purpose of this case or were they highlighted in Stakic -- or not in Stakic, in the case where he gave evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that these -- this is a photocopy of the issue that we had in the leadership unit. Someone from that unit had highlighted for whatever reason those particular points. It's highlighted by the OTP but I can't say for this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the writing in red, there is one which says nema fakture, and then some numbers, 151.050, 0 something 3, 3.050, 34, ARH, IV, maybe archive or something like that. What's that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm getting a copy so I can follow, Your Honour. Your Honour, I believe all of these were simply -- was writing made by persons who were making notes at various times. I don't think any of the handwriting should be considered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Sivac, is it correct that you had not seen this issue of Kozarski Vjesnik and these articles until you testified on the Stakic case, if I've given you the right articles?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see these. At the time when this issue came out, I was at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. But just to be complete, you have subsequently obtained other prior issues of Kozarski Vjesnik that were issued during the time you were in the camp, but you had not seen this particular issue and these particular articles to your knowledge until you testified in Stakic. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, in case it has just passed by without your noticing, you intended before I interrupted you to asking the witness to read part of this document. Did you mean -- did you intend him to read out loud so that we get a translation of the relevant part or just read for himself and then answer the questions that you were putting, going to put to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, I'm actually asking him -- well we have a translation, so it's up to Your Honours. But the translation of the particular article on this page, I believe, is the article -- appears on Exhibit 239, so it's 239A. Perhaps the witness can help me because at the moment I'm confused which of the articles this is the translation of. I could figure it out in time with my limited Cyrillic, but I think he could tell us much quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, on this first page do you see an article with the headline, "Visits Krajina Representatives in Prijedor"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the first one?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. That's the main news item on this page, except the commentary, "New International Order," which is to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could just put it on the ELMO and the witness will just point to the article he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will do that but it's abundantly clear that he's referring actually to the first article, top, top left, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We have the translation of that. I don't know if Your Honours would like it to be read; it's rather short. But that would be Exhibit S239A, and I would asking that S239A be admitted into evidence, the translation of that article, which is part of the redacted transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are we ready with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Shall I have the witness read it out loud for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there is a need for it. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no need for it, but don't we need to assign the exhibit different numbers from the Stakic numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will do that. I think we will follow the same procedure that we adopted previously in the course of the Stakic documents, before we broke for the holidays, and that would be the -- this number, Stakic, and then slash, the number of -- P19 whatever. Ms. Chuqing? That's not difficult, Mr. Ackerman. You want to know it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think for somebody who is reading the record in the future it's important to have the exhibit number at the same place the exhibit is discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not going to make that much difference because whichever number we give it, this number, the Stakic number, is going to feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it does not create any problem. Yes, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I had the same request as Mr. Ackerman. I'll refer to in my further examination as S239A as the Stakic number if we need to refer to. Can we now have the witness shown page 4 of that issue, which I believe is marked in the Stakic case S242/4. Could that be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And Mr. Sivac, if you could identify an article on that page concerning the visit of the delegation to the Omarska camp entitled "It's Difficult For Everyone."

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the heading of the article from the Kozarski Vjesnik, and it's dated the 17th of July, 1992. And the top heading is "Representatives of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the Banja Luka Municipality Visited Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of this article, it lists members of that delegation. Again, would it be correct that you had not seen this article until you testified on the Stakic case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is -- Mr. Koumjian, before he answers, could you direct us to the translation of this article?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the Stakic case S238A is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 238A, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My question again, Mr. Sivac, is: Is it correct that you had not seen this article until you testified in the Stakic case and until you had already described the persons that you had recognised in the delegation that visited the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this article later. Before that, I had just finished telling the story about the visit of the delegation of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina to the Omarska camp, and only after that I received this article to read. And that was the first time that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: To clarify something, because the judges do not have that portion of your transcript, is it correct that in the Stakic case, you had named the person who headed this delegation that had visited the Omarska camp before you saw these articles?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I identified completely the persons who were in that delegation, and I was given this article to read by representatives of the Prosecutor's Office and my memory still serves me well. All of those that I had mentioned were actually mentioned by the journalists also who wrote this article, so I was absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm interested right now in one particular individual. Who was the individual that you had testified, before reading this article, headed the delegation that arrived in July at the Omarska camp, the political delegation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The political delegation came to Omarska. The most prominent and the most important member of the delegation was the accused here, Radoslav Brdjanin. At that time, he was, I think, the President of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now have the exhibit from the Stakic case that was marked S15-2/I put on the ELMO. If Your Honours don't have it, you can use my copy. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Sivac, perhaps it's not necessary right at this moment to refer to this map or this photograph, but can you tell the judges in your own words, in July of 1992, you testified in Stakic, you were imprisoned in the Omarska camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And do you recall a day in July of that year where a delegation of high-ranking officials arrived, and can you tell Your Honours -- Their Honours about what happened that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: From the early morning, all the inmates were told to leave the rooms they were in. Milorad Tadic, Brk; Zeljko Meakic's, the camp commander's assistant, was in charge of lining us up together with the other guards and the heads of the -- the shift leaders, the guards' shift leaders, at the cement plateaus in front of the hangars, in front of the administrative building, where I was staying. I was in the room with Mujo Burho to be specific. And in front of the administrative building, in front of the garage, were the inmates from the garage. That's where they were lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps now you might turn to your right, to the photograph, and use that, if it's helpful to you, to describe the scene that day when the prisoners were taken out of the rooms.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is the hangar and then somewhere here in this area, where the pista is and the hangar plateau, the inmates were lined up. And then here in front of the administrative building, the inmates were also lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I was standing right here, and I marked the place with my initials, NS, somewhere in front of the administrative building so that I was in a very good position to see what would happen later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, the markings on this photograph, the blue initials, NS, you just pointed to and the red lines and there are some other blue ink marks, were those markings that you put on this photograph during your testimony in the Stakic case?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The whole morning, Milorad Tadic, Brk, practised with us the singing of Chetnik songs, and so that we would shout as loudly as possible, "This is Serbia, this is Serbia," and to raise three fingers in salute. We didn't know what was happening in the camp or what was going to happen. Around noon, along the main road to the Omarska mine from the main entrance towards the camp, we saw a long column of cars arriving. At the head of the column was a police car with rotating lights. It was an armoured vehicle, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, you pointed to the lower right of the photograph as the direction from which the vehicles arrived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if it might be helpful but do you know on this photograph, which direction north would be, just for -- perhaps to make it easier to refer to matters later?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is the north. This is actually the north. I think that's it. South is here and then west and east. North, east, west, and south. I know this very well because before I stayed at the Omarska camp or at the Omarska mine, I reported from the mine hundreds and hundreds of times, I reported on the successes of the employees. I followed the work of the mine practically from the time it started to operate, and I covered every new plant that was opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So just to make it clear, Mr. Sivac, please, the triangle which is at the bottom right of that photograph, points to which direction? To the -- no, the triangle, just move there, just below there. There is a dark triangle at the bottom right of the photo. It is very near where you are. No, no. Of the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The corner of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The corner of the photo, the bottom right corner. That is pointing to which direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the north, the north, the north. But this is a model.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So the triangle at the bottom right corner of the photo is indeed pointing towards the north? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So the delegation arrived from the north, and can you tell us again how those vehicles proceeded? What you saw from your position?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: After the APC, behind the APC, which was manned by members of the intervention detachment, who were situated in Prijedor, there was a vehicle where is Simo Drljaca was with his driver, Milorad Vokic and behind him was a car carrying Dusan Jankovic, who was the commander of the police in Prijedor. They jumped out of their cars very quickly and immediately joined the delegation, from the camp, which was headed by Zeljko Meakic, the camp commander, Milorad Tadic, Brk, and others, other guard shift leaders who were working at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before you move on, just to clarify, in your transcript in Stakic, you talked about the intervention squad and named two what you called prominent figures or notorious figures, Dado or Darko Mrdja and, I believe, Zoran Babin. Is that the same squad that you're referring to now?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were the best-known as well as the worst members, if I can put it that way, of the infamous intervention squad from the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these police and security people, can you describe other vehicles with members of the delegation that came?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Several other vehicles were there which were parked somewhere around the entrance, and then we started to recognise the people who were coming out of those vehicles. The first among those that I recognised was the accused here, Radoslav Brdjanin, who was accompanied by Radomir Vukic. The President of the main board of the Serbian Democratic Party for the region of Banja Luka. His nickname actually was Rale Monstrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Which translates -- I didn't get the translation of that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Rale Monstrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. You pointed to where the political -- the cars carrying the political leaders stopped and just so the record is clear, am I correct, you pointed to where there are two dots at the northern edge of the model? Is that correct? Right where you are right now? Thank you. I think the record is clear now. You said --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said you recognised Mr. Brdjanin. Can you tell us how you recognised Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Brdjanin before that in the newspapers or maybe in some TV programmes. He was performing the high function of the president of the Autonomous Region of the Bosnian Krajina of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. What happened after the politicians got out of or the honoured guests, whatever you referred to them as, got out of their vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: We were shouting, singing, when they came out of those vehicles. Radoslav Brdjanin approached with the Banja Luka delegation and the Prijedor political delegation, and he stood in front. And out of this group of people, representing the camp delegation, Zeljko Meakic made a few steps forward, the commander of the camp, and practically in a military way, reported and addressed Radoslav Brdjanin. He reported something to him on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Of all the people that you saw in that delegation, who was the first one that the camp commander Meakic reported to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, Zeljko Meakic saluted and reported to Radoslav Brdjanin, and behind him were other members of the Banja Luka political delegation, and the Prijedor political delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Earlier you talked about in the morning, Brk had you practising singing and you made a brief gesture that you were required to make and you raised your hand. The record would not be clear. Can you describe the gesture that you were forced to make for the delegation. Did you have to give them a type of salute?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is the conventional Serb greeting with three fingers. We had to put up our hand all the time and we had to sing very loudly and to shout out, "This is Serbia, this is Serbia." I have to explain to the Chamber the political delegation which came to the camp almost -- I mean almost all members of this delegation were laughing. They thought it was very funny how these personnel from the Omarska camp managed to coach us, to prepare us, for something like that. Amongst the inmates, there were also intellectuals and businessmen; that is, people who had some weight in the municipality of Prijedor, and unfortunately, at that time, they had to humiliate themselves and under pressure, against their own will, they had to sing and utter words which were deeply offensive to the ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, this is the middle of July of 1992. Can you describe the appearance of the prisoners who were lined up to greet the Banja Luka delegation.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, we looked pretty miserably. Almost all the inmates had torture marks, harassment, ill treatment marks, and we'd already been marked by all that we had gone through in the Omarska camp. Many inmates had no foot wear. A number of us also did not have all the parts of clothing. The speciality of the Omarska guards was to snatch away, be it footwear or perhaps parts of clothes from the inmates, so that many people were barefoot, and naked waist up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did any of the prisoners, to your recollection, have any bandages and if so, can you describe what was used for these bandages?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Why, yes. Many inmates had all sorts of bandages, some make shift bandages which Dr. Enes [as interpreted] Sadikovic used to make from parts of our underwear. He would tear up this underwear and use it as bandages to protect, at least a little bit, some of the injuries we had sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please, the first name of Dr. Sadikovic, it was translated as Enes. Can you correct that.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Dr. Esad Sadikovic, an UNHCR expert, a doctor, a specialist, who treated people all his life irrespective of their faith or colour of their skin. Before that he was in Africa as an UNHCR expert on western Samoa in the Pacific, and he returned to Prijedor on the eve of the war. And from there, he was rounded up when the camp was founded and unfortunately killed him on the 7th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, and you discuss that in your first testimony very thoroughly. Going back to the delegation, can you tell us what they did once they got out of the cars, and in particular, most importantly, please tell us what you recall Mr. Brdjanin doing after he emerged from the vehicle and was saluted by Meakic.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: After that ceremony, if I may call it that, the political delegation headed by Brdjanin moved in this direction and I think he halted somewhere here and he tried to say something briefly, but I couldn't hear that, because -- because we were singing very loudly and shouting those famous slogans so I suppose only those in the front line could hear him, if they heard him. And after a brief delay there, the delegation headed by Brdjanin and others Simo Drljaca and others, took this path towards the administration building to the fetching up at the entrance to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could try to describe what the witness pointed out on the map. He indicated a route along the red line which would be on the east side of the administrative building, the first building, on the northern part of the picture, travelling in a southerly direction. He indicated Mr. Brdjanin stopped at a point where there is a blue dot and attempted to address, say something. He said after that, the delegation continued, and he drew a somewhat circular motion which follows the blue arrow that's drawn in ink that's just outside the red lines. Would that be correct, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just mention, I'm sorry, the ceremony, Zeljko Meakic's report took place here at these two points right here. Because these dots mark the places where the masts were with flags, with very large flags. One was the Serb flag with four S's, and the other one was the flag of new Yugoslavia, as they called it, that was the conventional tri-colour without the five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Indicating again the two dots at the northern edge of the photograph, lower right of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, at that time, in the Omarska camp, you were not wearing your glasses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. That is, I had glasses. I started needing -- I needed glasses only for reading but it was only 0.25 or 0.50, so it wasn't a large optics. My eye sight deteriorated suddenly five years ago because in the meantime after all that I had suffered there, I contracted diabetes, high sugar content, and that has been my chief problem over the past five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The map has red lines on it which I presume, correct me if I'm wrong, are where the prisoners lined up. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It is, yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct then that the prisoners were lined up in addition to in front of the administration building, in front of the garage, and in front of the white house? To the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, in the -- in my Stakic case testimony, I drew those lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And one other matter, perhaps should be clarified. In the Stakic case, you were asked before -- you were asked when you first testified to view six individuals one of which was Dr. Stakic, and you identified him from those six individuals. You correctly identified him. Is that true? The guy you identified is the one who remained in the court and sat down next to Defence counsel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to go now then -- I'm finished with that photograph -- to matter that was not covered in -- much in your testimony in Stakic. Do you recall the day that the foreign journalists first visited the Omarska camp, Penny Marshall and Vulliamy and Williams?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I recall it. It was the August the 5th, if I'm correct. And that day, early in the morning, in front of the building that I was in at Mujo Burho, that is in front of that garage, we heard some noise, we heard people talking and some guards turned up and ordered that in front of the administrative building and the garage where we were, that there had to be complete silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago Dr. Eso Sadikovic, and you mentioned him in further detail in your Stakic testimony. Do you recall what happened with Dr. Sadikovic that day, the day that the journalists were to arrive?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: After that order that we had to keep complete silence, that nobody was even to hear that there was somebody in those buildings, they after all that, they called out Dr. Esad Sadikovic and took him away. Dr. Eso Sadikovic was taken out very often. He went to extend medical aid even to guards who came to the camp, drunk, and would wound each other, and that is because of the frequent robbery or mugging of the prisoners. They would start quarrelling. They were start arguing over the booty. And they treated each other very roughly. Quite often, they were also highly intoxicated and then they would fire the weapons that they all had and would wound one another. They took Dr. Eso away and brought him -- brought him back only late at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Dr. Sadikovic speak any foreign language?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Why, yes, of course, he was fluent in English because, being an UNHCR expert and a doctor, and a physician, a member of the medicine san frontier, he frequently stayed for prolonged periods of time in other countries where he had to speak English and I think he was also quite conversant in French. And I think he was learning Spanish because he was waiting to go to a country where that language was spoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you have any information, based upon your knowledge of Dr. Sadikovic, whether you believe he would have been an articulate and effective spokesman for the persons in Omarska, interned in Omarska, and for the non-Serb population of Prijedor, had he been able to speak to the world media?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Eso was very, very sociable. He had an a very broad vocabulary and he also enjoyed charisma. He enjoyed a status of a highly accomplished intellectual, and I think that it was because of that that Dr. Eso Sadikovic was removed, fearing that he might establish contact with those journalists who had come, in order to conceal all the things that were going on in the camp. Your Honours, I have to tell you that it was only after I left Bosnia and went to a western country that I saw on television this story about Penny Marshall and Ed Williams' visit. I cried when I saw it because in that story, in that footage, I saw how -- how -- in what an ugly manner and how fiercely Simo Drljaca is explaining to journalists what fantastic treatment we were enjoying in the camp and that they were green berets, all around the camp, that is Muslim fighters and we in that camp had all the food that we needed, all the water that we needed, that we were accommodated well that we were practically in hotels or in some resort or something, yet the reality was quite different, and it was very ugly indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In those broadcasts you mentioned that Drljaca told them that there were green berets surrounding Omarska, and you may have seen that he told this them that they were in danger visiting the camp. At that time, in August, August the 5th of 1992, on that day, or prior days, did the guards at the camp show any concern with being shot at from the woods or from the area surrounding Omarska? Did they appear to act as if they thought there were green berets, surrounding the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: True, I saw Simo Drljaca's escort Vokic, is acting in that programme. He puts up a performance about how he's -- at the very entrance at Omarska how he's running and sort of firing in some direction because allegedly the green berets were somewhere in that direction, trying, I guess, to attack this convoy with journalists and with Simo Drljaca, at the head. But it was all a put-on. Towards the end of June, the ethnic cleansing had been completed. That is all the non-Serbs in those areas had been removed and the Omarska camp is -- was surrounded by Serb villages, they were all Serb villages around it. So there was no way for anyone to come near the camp -- I mean, aside from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Based upon your experience in the camp, although -- am I correct that you then never saw the foreign journalists? You were kept inside the room throughout their visit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. We were inside, in this room. We were given nothing to eat, not even water, and we had to keep very quiet because we'd been threatened, if any -- if one could hear any sound, that is shout or any sign indicating that there were people in that room, that we'd suffer consequences the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said, though, that subsequently, you saw the broadcasts and am I correct you also saw the journalists go to Trnopolje and broadcasts of photographs smuggled to the journalists by Dr. Idriz Merdzanic and Azra Blazevic? Can you tell us if that visit and those broadcasts, if you noticed an effect upon the lives of the people in Omarska and in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, we were kept inside. We were not aware of that visit that day. As I said, this footage was screened several years later again. But after this delegation's visit -- I mean after the journalists' visit, those two journalists, we realised that something unreal was happening in the Omarska camp, that is the guards who had been so rough, who treated us so basically all of a sudden started behaving differently. We simply couldn't understand that they had all of a sudden started talking with us, because until then it was simply inconceivable. And we couldn't understand what was going on, why that complete change in the conduct of the guards and people who worked in the camp administration, in the way they treated us. We simply couldn't comprehend what had happened. And only later, a few days later, that is, after we had been transferred to the Trnopolje camp, we -- it was only then that we learned about that visit and it was thanks to a group of very brave journalists, headed by Penny Marshall and Vulliamy, I think that the lives of many inmates were saved thanks to their visit, and I claim this quite openly because my contacts in the Omarska camp, with the Mlado Radic, Krkan, a man whom I'd known almost all my life and who was one -- the head of one of the worst shifts, when he saw me in the Omarska camp for the first time, he was very surprised and said, "Sivi," that's my nickname, "I can't help you here. All of you who are here are intended for liquidation." I understood what he meant by that. In a contact when I was going for a meal, and food was being distributed by my sister, who was also in the Omarska camp, together with those other 36 women from Prijedor, and I told her briefly that Krkan had said that we would all be liquidated. And she almost cried, but I had to leave straight away. And later on, through Zeljko Meakic, the camp commander, whom she knew very well from different court cases because my sister was a Judge in the Court in Prijedor, and she asked Zeljko if I was to be taken away to be shot, she asked Zeljko if they could kill her instead, because she had -- she was single and I had a wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: A day or two after the foreign journalists' visit, two days later, you were released, along with many others, to Trnopolje? Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 12764 to 12772.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In your testimony in Stakic, you talked about Dr. Eso Sadikovic being taken away and all the members of your room standing to salute him. When was that in relation to the visit of the foreign journalists?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It was a few days -- no, a day or two after the journalists' visit. Namely after the journalists' visit, the nights in Omarska were eerily quiet because nobody was being called out, taken away, nobody was liquidated. There was no firing. And sometime towards the dawn break, very early in the morning, suddenly the door opened with a bang and a guard said, "Dr. Eso Sadikovic, come out." We were at a loss. We thought they were taking him again to help somebody, to tend to somebody. But then they told him to take all his belongings with him and then we saw light. Dr. Eso stood up and he was in the bottom of the room that we were in. He picked up his plastic bag, in which he had a dirty shirt and I think some cigarette butts which the inmates had collected around the camp for him because he was an impassioned smoker, and he slowly started towards the exit. And at that moment, those who were awake and those who were asleep also woke up and stood up and in a chorus, loudly started crying -- shouting, "Doctor, thank you for all that you've done." Doctor, I think was well aware of where they were taking him and we were also well aware of that. When he reached the door, he turned and he only said, "Goodbye, friends." We couldn't really grasp that at that moment, there was a man in the world who could kill such a man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, you showed me a newspaper article from Kozarski Vjesnik which I told you I had not seen before in which it had a photograph of Dr. Sadikovic. And is it correct that in this Kozarski Vjesnik articling he's listed as among those favouring the Gandhian way of peace, the moderates, among the Muslims in Prijedor, and this is an issue from after the Serb takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we take this up after the break, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Witness, please answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Dr. Eso and a large number of Prijedor intellectuals of Bosniak and Croat origin organised some -- organised rallies for peace. He was indeed a man who didn't think much of violence and solution of problems in a violent manner. He always advocated the Gandhian way of solving problems for Muslims and other people in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The only other matters I have to deal with would be the exhibits from the Stakic testimony which we could even do -- I'll get together with Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. See if you could come together in the break for a short while so we'll pave the way for a smoother second session. We'll now break for 25 minutes, is that suitable for what you need to do? And we will resume immediately after that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the record, perhaps an explanation to the public is in order to explain why we are starting 30 minutes or even more after. There was some documents that the Defence needed very urgently and time was required to obtain them. So we are now in a position to resume the examination-in-chief and then Mr. Ackerman will follow with the cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I did say I had no further questions, but over that long break I thought of a few others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said you had some questions or you wanted to refer the witness to some documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, we can go over the documents, I suggest we -- we can do that either now or after he testifies. The admission of the documents that were referred to in the Stakic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But I have a few questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a question that we would like to put to the witness before Mr. Ackerman takes over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I do have a few questions also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: First, Mr. Sivac, you mentioned Mr. Esad Sadikovic. Do you know if he had a wife and family and if so, what the ethnicity of his wife was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Eso Sadikovic's wife was a Serb. Her name is Zorica. She is somewhere from Serbia. She still lives in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did he have children with her?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, two children. He had a daughter called Alma and a son called Eniz. At the time when Dr. Eso Sadikovic was killed, his daughter was 15 years old and his son was 11. I would just like to note that Dr. Eso Sadikovic's son Eniz is the same age as my daughter, and they went to school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And another matter that I just a few moments ago occurred to me I forgot to ask you about. After your release from the Omarska camp, and Trnopolje, did you ever see the accused, Mr. Brdjanin, on television after that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: After I left, Mr. Brdjanin, the accused here, together with a very good acquaintance of mine, Srdjo Srdic, who was the leader of the Serbian Democratic Party from Prijedor, took part in a political programme on Serb television in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Srdic was actually a representative to the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later, when the split --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The Serb assembly, the Serb parliament, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct he was actually elected to the Bosnian parliament and then when the Serbs left that parliament and formed their own, he joined the Serb parliament?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Please describe what you recall about that programme and what was said, particularly by the accused, Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The programme lasted for more than an hour and it was open to receive questions from viewers. And as far as I remember, the gist of the programme was that the accused here, Radoslav Brdjanin, commended the Prijedor Crisis Staff and political leadership for having done a very good job in the territory of the Prijedor municipality, that they cleansed the area very well in accordance to some plans. And I remember very well a sentence that he used, and it was a sentence often used by someone who shares his political views, and who worked with him, Radoslav Lukic, known as Rale Monster, Rale Monstrum [Realtime transcript read in error "Radoslav Lukic]. Brdjanin repeated a sentence then, that all -- and the sentence is as follows: "All the non-Bosniaks who remained to live there, he said all Turks or balijas who remain in the territory of the Serbian state will shake with fear. Their pants will shake with fear, if they do not accept the laws of the Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just one clarification, the transcript and when you discussed Rale Monstrum translated the name as Radoslav Lukic. Can you correct the last name of this individual.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Radoslav Vukic [Realtime transcript read in error "Vukovic"], with a "V."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. Your Honours indicated you had one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Gentlemen, before you start, Mr. Ackerman, we have a very simple question actually. Mr. Sivac, I refer you to previous part of your testimony. You had mentioned Zeljko Meakic, you had mentioned Mlado Radic. Was Mlado Radic also known as Krkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What position did he occupy, that you know of? You referred to this person as someone that you had known almost all your life. So when you met him on the occasion that you referred to before, I was surprised to see you there in Omarska, what position did he occupy then? What was his official function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mlado Radic, known as Krkan, an acquaintance of mine, I've known him practically all my life, he was most of the time heading the worst guard shift. During their watch, most of the killings and rapes took place. And I would like to say that there has been a mistake again. It should say "Radoslav Vukic" and not "Radoslav Vukovic." At least that's what I see on my transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mlado a member of the police or some organisation that you know of, at the time that he told you that the inmates there in Omarska were meant to -- were intended for liquidation? Was he a member of the police then? Or what was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a member of the police force, an active police officer, at the Omarska Police Station, until he was appointed commander, one of the guard shifts in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start, Mr. Ackerman is the lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. Your duty here as a witness is to answer his questions the same way you answered the questions from the Prosecution. You have no right to discriminate in favour or against any one of the officials here. He is here in an official function and he has the responsibility and duty to defend his client. Therefore, he's got every right to ask questions to you and you have an absolute duty to answer each and every question as truthfully and as fully as you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to personally apologise to you for the delay that was occasioned a few moments ago and tell you that it was completely my fault. But I'm sorry for that. The result of that is that the time I have to cross-examine you is shortened, and the only way that we can get that done is if you cooperate with me by answering the questions as -- in as brief a way as possible. And if I want you to explain further about some answer, then I can ask you to do that. Would that be fair to you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I will do my best to give brief answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, one of the things I'm going to be doing is referring to some prior statements that you made, and you of course have an absolute right to look at those statements and confirm that what I'm saying you said is correct, but I would like to not do that, because of the time it takes, unless you believe it's absolutely necessary for you to do so. And you'll certainly have that right if you believe it's necessary. I want to begin my questioning of you by referring to one of those statements which comes out of a 17 February 2002 telephone conversation that you had with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and in that conversation, you were being asked about the persons who were part of this delegation that you have testified about here today. And in the course of naming the persons, you failed to name Radoslav Vukic. You were then reminded that you mentioned Dr. Vukic in an earlier statement I believe your 1994 statement. Do you remember that exchange during your telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I made many phone calls, specially with the Prosecutor's Office, and this was often done without the presence of an interpreter. When I testified in the Stakic case, I said that many of those conversations, the telephone conversations that I had, I do not accept because they were conducted without an interpreter under special circumstances. Quite often, I had -- held those conversations while I was driving my car. So at those times, I was not able to fully concentrate, simply the representatives from the Prosecutor's Office got to me while I was on the road and I usually try to keep those conversations as brief as possible because I was in the middle of driving. So at those times, I perhaps did not mention some of those people who were in the delegation that toured the camp. Secondly, I was never able to look and read through and correct any of those statements that I had given over the telephone. Last time I was here in July, I was taken unawares. And to give you a specific answer to your question, I accept the first statement that I gave in 1994. This statement was the most correct, and even since that time, nine years have passed. But at the time that I gave the statement my memory, my recollection, was quite fresh and all of the things that I had lived through while I was in the Omarska and Trnopolje camps were still fresh in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you finally at the end of your answer, sort of made the point that I was labouriously going to get to and that is that the things in your earlier statements, your 1994 statement, are likely to be your best recollection of the events. That's a fair statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Although I looked at that statement of mine for the first time after six years, and in that statement, some of the things that I said were quite badly translated, but I believe that they do not affect my overall statement that much, nor the substance of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you're doing what I hoped you would not do so that we could finish today, and that is your giving me much longer answers than my question calls for. If you really try not to do, we'll finish today. Otherwise you'll be here in the morning.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to do my part to try to finish today. I need your cooperation. In your book --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all right. In your book about -- I'm going to a different subject now -- in your book that's the Carsija u Prijedor u book, and I'm referring to the English summary only, page 22, I'm just going to tell you what that English summary says, sir. "Mirzat continues his story and gives an account of the retreat of the remains of Korevska Ceta Kurevo companies. In his opinion, the blame for what happened in Prijedor lies with the leader of the SDA who betrayed their own people." Now, my first question is who is Mirzat?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mirzat is my neighbour from Prijedor. He lives somewhere in [redacted] today and I don't know, Your Honour, I can reveal his identity. His name is [redacted], and he lives in [redacted]. So I hope that will not create any problems for him. And he used to be my neighbour in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps just in the interests of caution, we should redact the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it will be. The whereabouts of this person will be redacted. His name, however, will be retained in the transcript as stated by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what it means that the SDA later betrayed his own people?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: In the political biography of Mirza Mujadzic the leader of the SDA party in Prijedor, and many people are upset with him. There is a stain on that biography. I don't know if you had the opportunity -- and I need to be a little more detailed here, not too long though, I don't know if you ever saw the Radio Prijedor audio cassettes in which three years later, Simo Miskovic, the leader of the Serbian Democratic Party publicly talks about how the 30th of April, which is a key date in the destruction of the Prijedor municipality. On that day, Mr. Mujadzic came to the barracks to see Captain Arsic and Lieutenant Zeljaja, and in the presence of the SDA leader, practically reached an agreement to hand over power in Prijedor without firing one bullet, and this is what it was like, Mr. Attorney. Many friends believe, many people in Prijedor believe that with that act, Mirza Mujadzic betrayed his own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Referring again to the Carsija book, and this is page 55 of the English summary, there is a section in your book where you talk about Muslims who committed crimes against their own people. And what you said was, if this summary is correct, "It is not often mentioned that some of the Muslims committed despicable crimes against their own people. Some of them were even more cruel than Serbs." And then you give a list of 15 people who you claim were part of that group. And I'd like to go through that list as briefly as we can. The first one on the list is Sead Besic, and you indicate that he was from Kozarac, that he was loyal to the new Serbian state and worked for the SDB, he denounced and disarmed Bosniaks and Croats and played a key role in overthrowing the legally elected government of the SDA and HDZ and bringing the SDS to power. After a genocide in the region of Prijedor he was promoted and moved to the security service centre in Banja Luka where he remains to the present day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Shortly afterwards, he had -- he was forced to retire and there was no longer any work for him in the Public Security Services in Banja Luka, and I think that today he's living in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the second person on the list is Hamdija Handzic. He was a major in the JNA apparently, an artillery major. His artillery units destroyed houses and killed people you say in Kostajnica, Jasenovac, Lipik, Pakrac, Kozarac, Prijedor and the surrounding villages of Carakovo, Hambarine, and Borcani --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He also destroyed houses and killed people in Gradacac, Orasje, Brcko, Bihac, Bosanska Krupa, correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Hamdija Hadzic called Mikula, little Mikola. A very good acquaintance of mine. I was surprised when in reporting for TV Sarajevo in 1991 from the front in Croatia, in an artillery regiment, I was surprised when I saw Hamdija Hadzic. Everything was clear to me. Sead Besic is married to a Serb. Hamdija Hadzic also, so they have mixed marriages. Even though I have nothing against mixed marriages, a large number of people who lived -- who had married Serb women accepted the ideology at that time which was conducted at that time by the Serbian authorities, and they expressed loyalty and actively participated in the killing of their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 3 is a person named Zijad Music, aka Ziko?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Not Ziko, I apologise, but Ziko. He is one of the most notorious members of the infamous elite squad which was called "el manijakos." I would like to have a proper translation of that term "el manijakos," which were equipped and trained by Radmilo Zeljaja and they acted as part of the 343rd Motorised Brigade in Croatia, and then that Brigade was just called the 43rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The translation of "el manijakos" is the maniacs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. And that is how they behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 4 is Asmir Music, a Serbian volunteer, destroyed and among other things set the house of HM on fire, took part in the mass killings during the cleansing of the villages surrounding Prijedor in Croatia and BH. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Asmir Muhic is the son of Husein Zika [phoen]. He also participated in that. He's a cousin of Sia Music Zika [phoen], so sometimes they acted together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 5 is Zlatan Blazevic, who you say was the founder and commander of the "los manijakos," the maniacs, and he specialized in killing, chronic alcoholic, looter, and killer. True?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Zlatan Blazevic, yes, the son of Anto, a Croat and his mother was a Muslim, was also a member of -- "el manijakos." And in one action they conducted somewhere in the corridor, he was killed sometime in 1992 and 1993, in late 1992 or in early 1993. But his own brother, Atko Blazevic came in his place and he's also on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So Atko is number 6 on the list and you've already mentioned him so --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. He's the brother of Zlatan Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will now go to number 7, Emsud Sabic, aka, Sabo, a cafe owner was a volunteer financed the Chetnik unit of Zoran Karlica, took part in mass killings around Gradacac and Orasje, Bihac and Derventa, permanent sponsor and supplier of the Serbian army, provides them with food and cigarettes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Sabic shabo is a well known merchant in Prijedor and he owns a coffee shop. He's also married to a close cousin of Zoran Karlica.
