One of the commanders in the 343 or the 43rd Motorised Brigade of Radmilo Zeljaja and he actively participated in the fighting around Gradacac, Brod, Derventa, and other places where the Prijedor Brigade acted, the Prijedor Serb Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 8 is Sabahudin Zulic, you describe as a Chetnik and member of Zoran Karlica's unit, distinguished itself in atrocities and murders in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, destroyed Stari Grad, Lukavica, Partizankska Street, M. Suljanovica Street in Prijedor, destroyed villages near Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. He didn't live in Partizankska Street but he lived near the Parisankso cemetery and he was the closest neighbour of Zoran Karlica and he was also his work colleague. They went to war together in Croatia to fight together in Croatia, and after that, they went to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 9 is Goran Egrlic, Serbian volunteer at all fronts in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, personal driver and body guard of Vladimir Arsic and Radmilo Zeljaja, two notorious Chetnik officers, correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Goran Ergerlic, son of Husad [phoen] and mother Dragica [phoen], that is his father is Muslim and his mother is Serb, up to the war, that is until 1992, he worked as a driver at the SDK service. And when the war started, when the war in Croatia started, when the Brigade under the command of Radmilo Zeljaja went against Croatia because he was his driver of Zeljaja's and his personal escort, he was slightly wounded. That is I have to mention him, that in Croatia somewhere around the Pakrac or Pikan [phoen], there was an attack on Radmilo Zeljaja, an assassination attempt, but they managed to get out alive. They survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 10 is Fatima Kararic a professor at grammar school in Prijedor. You say about her that she used to break in and loot abandoned apartments and move Chetniks in. She personally evicted her Bosniak and Croatian colleagues. Then you say, She is responsible for the ethnic cleansing in the region of Prijedor, an accomplice in the murder of the professors of the grammar school, Muhammed Cehajic, Fikret Mujkic, Latif Benic, and Husein Crnkic. True?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Fatima Kararic, a Muslim, is a person who worked as a teacher in the grammar school and she was married to a Serb man. His last name was Sipovac, and he worked in the Prijedor military department. And I remember very well that in 1991, when she organised at the Prijedor grammar school two lines of children who threw flowers on the Prijedor Brigade led by Radmilo Zeljaja and Zoran Karlica who were returning from the Croatian front. They were having orgies in the streets of Prijedor. They were firing in the streets. And Fatima Kararic, together with her followers people who thought the same as her in the Prijedor grammar school, she then used these children from the school to throw flowers and the brigade and the troops the soldiers who were coming back from Croatia where they had killed Croatian people. In the Omarska camp, counsel -- I'll be very brief. In the Omarska camp, teacher Fikret Mujakic was killed, teacher Husein Crnkic, and the head master of the Prijedor grammar school where Fatima Kararic worked and Latif Benic. So I would just like to mention these three. And they were killed and a life story, their biography, Fatima Kararic accused them of some imaginary things and their life was cut short in the camp of Omarska. They were killed in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 11 is Ernest Badnjevic who you say from the beginning of the war wore a Chetnik uniform and provided services for the Chetnik army through the integral firm of which he was a joint owner, correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a special duty. He would assign for the Radmilo Zeljaja Brigade he would decide on all the propaganda tasks. And he wore a uniform and he even went to wage war somewhere in -- on the front, somewhere in Bosnia or in Croatia. He used to be a youth official in the Prijedor municipality. He was a member of the SK committee. Counsel, I'd just have to stress that this is a lot longer list, but I have just put in the book people who were the most prominent, those who were known by the most people in Prijedor. There should be some additional lists but not many, during those times. However, many Muslims, Bosniaks, Croats, they were aware of what they can expect, and they did not want to buckle under pressure or, God forbid, accept the humiliation to accept the Serb or Chetnik ideology, which we can see in this list, some of them did accept it in order to save their own skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have four more. Let's get through them as quickly as we can, please. Zlatan Crnalic was a pilot in the Serbian air force?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Zlatan Crnalic, again my neighbour on that list, most people are my neighbours. This is son of Hajro. Before 1992 he was active in the army. He was used to be a pilot in the Yugoslav air force, and he flew from Berovica Slavonja on a plane. He flew into the Banja Luka airport. He became loyal to the Serb authorities, and he became a pilot in the Serb air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in that process did some bombing, you say he bombed Bihac, Cazin, Kladusa, Krupa, Travnik, Vlasic, and in that process killed numerous innocent civilians.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. He was active in the air force of the Republika Srpska, and it is well known where and which parts of Bosnia this air force was active during the conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 13 is Muhamed Sarajlic. He was a reserve policeman who you say signed a certificate of loyalty to Serbian authorities and wearing a uniform of Serbian police took part in the ethnic cleansing in Prijedor region and the deportation of people in the camps. True?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 14 is Sead Alajbegovic. He remained loyal to Serbian authorities after he signed the certificate of loyalty. Became their main supplier of food and cigarettes, donated large amounts of foreign currency, money was used for salaries?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Finally number 15, Zlatan Selimbegovic, a Serbian volunteer, wore the Chetnik uniform, and has been on all fronts in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the Chetnik army committed crimes. Okay? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to go to a different subject now. I want to talk about how the camp at Omarska was created. In your original 1994 statement to the Prosecutor, you told the people who you were talking to that a gentleman by the name of Milan Andjic was one of the people behind the setting up of the Omarska camp. And then earlier, in 1993, in a statement you made in Zagreb, you said, "The extremists that organised and financed the Omarska detention camp were Milan Andjic, a shopkeeper from Omarska, and owner of the Trias tavern, Nedjo Delic, owner of two restaurants called Europe, one in Prijedor and the other in Omarska. The name of the commander of their paramilitary formations which they organised and financed was Nenad Radanovic, AKA, Cigo, who killed several hundred civilians during the cleansing of Kozarac." Let me first ask you what you know about this person Cigo?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Nenad Radanovic, also known as Cigo, he used to be, before the war, a taxi driver in Prijedor. He was a close friend of -- that is his senior friend and colleague was Nenad Andjic, a merchant from Omarska, a very influential man in this area. When the war in Croatia started in 1991, Milan Andjic personally because he was a very rich man, he collected a group of young men from Omarska and the Prijedor area and he personally dressed them and they were armed by the then army, the Yugoslav army. They were -- they underwent special training at the Manjaca training ground and they took part in the war in Croatia as a special elite unit from Omarska. A large amount of looted things from Croatia, which this unit under the command of Nenad Radanovic, Cigo, brought -- they were brought to Omarska to the very large yard of Milan Andjic. That's where they were brought. In that yard, he sold building material and other things, kitchen appliances. Later on, Milan Andjic managed to sell all these things through his shops while Radanovic continued to take part in combat in various fronts near corridor, in Derventa, in Gradacac, and other fronts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And one of the darkest plots in his operations was the ethnic cleansing of the right side, so to speak, of the villages that are neighbouring Kozarac. During the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac, and the villages that are linked to Kozarac, Jakupovici, Brdjani, a large number of civilians were killed, women and children, and on that side, along this direction, it was the brigade of Nenad Radanovic, Cigo, which was involved on that side, and he is thought to have committed many crimes that were committed there, a large number of crimes. You asked me further on about Nenad Radanovic, Cigo, what I know about him. I know that later on in the Prijedor municipality, he became one of the vice-presidents of the Prijedor municipality, precisely thanks to his war achievements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A statement that you made to German authorities, you were asked about the two people we've mentioned, Andjic and Delic that you described as people responsible for setting up Omarska camp, and you said the following: "Both those individuals are influential business people from the area --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down when reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Both those individuals are influential business people from the area and are almost the most important politicians there. Both were responsible for ensuring that the Serbian population formed the proper judgement of the Muslims, that is they were the intellectuals who were responsible for shaping opinion. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is all completely incorrect, sir. I don't understand that, sir. I've known them for such a long time. I would never have said that, that they were intellectuals. They are merchants, profiteers. They had their own bars, restaurant. I never said that they had established a camp. These were the people who financed some of those camps in part. That is completely untrue. I don't believe that I could have stated such a thing, particularly not in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you said in your 1994 statement to the OTP that Milan Andjic was one of the people behind the setting up of Omarska camp, were you misquoted? Was that a bad translation? Or what do you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: 1994, I said that Milan Andjic was one of the people who financed and organised the camp, yes. His task was, given by the Crisis Staff, was to organise the camp, to supply the food that we in fact got only once a day. He often came to the Omarska camp. Let me just tell you and only at night, sometime from midnight onwards. He took out Dedo Crnalic, who used to be a business partner of his from Prijedor, and for many nights they spoke together. Dedo was together with me in the premises, and he was a good friend of mine. So I asked him, what have you got to talk to Milan Andjic about when we although that Milan Andjic was one of the organisers of this camp, that he was one of his biggest sponsors, but Dedo was an elderly man, he was my heave and he said, well, I have to speak to someone to find out what will happen to us in this camp. Unfortunately, that Crnalic was killed on the 7th of August, in the convoy of camp prisoners who were being taken to Manjaca. And counsel, let me just ask you something. I apologise. This statement given in Zagreb, I don't know who I gave that to. Was that some centre for information with the Croatian government? And Jadrinka Sigim [phoen] may have take then statement, who was a co-prisoner of mine in the camp, who then started to work for the information centre in Zagreb. And she started to forge our statements to give false statements regarding our stay in the camp, and she was -- she was diminishing everything that happened to us in 1992 in order to put forward her own Croatian belonging. So I completely would like to distance myself from this statement, and I would request to have a look at it again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm showing you the statement that I was referring to and I don't know where it came from. The translation doesn't really tell us. Maybe you'll recognise it. Maybe you won't.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I can't find that. On which page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you looking for the quote that I gave you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the quote. I'm really interested?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On the English version it was on page 5. It begins with: "The extremists that organised and financed the Omarska detention camp were Milan Andjic," and then it goes on from there.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's correct. Extremists, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You found it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I haven't quite found it. This, what is said here, something is a little confused here. Could you just give me the code number below, please? What I have, the last 3 number, 746, 747, 748, 749, 750, the last three numbers of the code number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you have the document and I don't so I can't find -- I'm looking at the English version.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Can you just repeat, if you don't mind, if you can repeat your question so that I can answer you? What I said and what I remember and have always said and I stand by it, is that Milan Andjic was in charge of this camp and Nedjo Delic, somewhat less, and that Andjic was the most responsible political person. Everybody listened to him in Omarska. He was the one who was financing and organising it, and the main organiser is well known. These were the civilian authorities of the municipality of Prijedor, and this is what I said like in the Stakic case and Milomir Stakic was one of the responsible. These were the civilian authorities of the Prijedor municipality who were responsible for it. If you don't have that statement, I have, so I can give you one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in the 1993 statement in Zagreb, that you have before you now, sir, it is correct that --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- That that statement at least indicates that you said: "The extremists that organised and financed the Omarska detention camp were Milan Andjic, a shopkeeper from Omarska and owner of the Trias tavern, Nedjo Delic, owner of two restaurants called Europe, one in Prijedor the other in Omarska." That's at least what the statement says that you said, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct. Yes, that's what I'm saying now. That's what I stand by today. In all of these statements, I mentioned these people. That means that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The statement I'm actually more interested at this point is the one you gave to German authorities, and I now want to hand you that one. I want to refer you to page 6 and I've made a little mark there where the paragraph starts that I'm interested in. You see that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's your position that there is something not correct about that, true?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: A large part of this statement has not been translated correctly. As far as I remember, the interpreter, when I was giving the statement, this was an interpreter, a Croat woman, who had lived for many years in Germany, her name was Blazenkovic, and I never read this statement. This is some kind of a shortened version. And everything that you can see here has been taken out of the context of my statement. So my statements were shortened. They were edited so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you say that these people, Andjic and Delic, were responsible for shaping opinion?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. Not opinion. They were responsible for establishing a camp. But they were influential. Nedo -- Andjic was just an ordinary village politician. They were not intellectuals, I don't understand how this could have entered into my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to go back now to your book, the Carsija book. That book, under a heading called, "Calm before the storm," you wrote this: "No sooner than the war broke out, Milan Andjic formed his own paramilitary unit. Momcilo Radanovic aka, Cigo, a former taxi driver was appointed its commander. The long-held dream of the Omarska peasants to take over Prijedor finally came true." My question is: What is this long-held dream of the Omarska peasants to which you refer?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Mr. Ackerman. My answer -- for my answer I would have to go back into history, into the history of the Prijedor municipality, and that would need a lot of time here, but to cut the long story short, Omarska -- what has been a characteristic Chetnik region, and I think that you perhaps understand what that means. It had a deep Chetnik tradition, and it has always been region which did not accept, although they were part of the Prijedor municipality, frequently they had some kind of rebellions, they rebelled against the legally elected authority in Prijedor in communist times. They simply frequently refused to accept, and publicly said that if a Muslim was to head the Prijedor municipality, for them that was incomprehensible. They used pejorative terms. They did not want to accept authority in Prijedor municipality if led by a Turk, which is a derogatory for a Muslim, and I can list here countless examples when I reported in my very rich journalistic experience and I can mention just one incident. When the Omarska mine was founded, which was made in the local commune of Omarska, I was told by one of the leaders, Milan Andjic or someone else that practically all of them, and just them, would be working in the Omarska mine. They couldn't accept that in these mine, which was one of the most modern in Europe, would have to be employing experts who knew about the exploitation of mines. They kept saying that only people from Omarska would be working there regardless of their training and there were incidents that villages in Omarska, very frequently created incidents that the water supply was needed for the -- was cut, which was needed for the technological process and they were protesting because allegedly they had not been given a job in the mine. Their tendency and I do know that, that for a while this was a little freer, the way that they were start stating what they wanted is that the local commune of Omarska and many villages surrounding Omarska, they were even writing petitions, demanding for their area to be attached to Banja Luka, where Serbs had the authority, where Serbs were in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, I want to talk just ask you one question about the running of Omarska and Trnopolje. In your testimony in the Stakic case in July, page 6.753, you were asked about the role of the army in the running of Omarska, and you said this, "I don't know what the chain of command was. I'm not familiar with that. But as a prisoner, I had the impression that they didn't have any business connections with the camp. In Omarska, as well as Trnopolje, and Keraterm, there were not soldiers, and that's why I think that the army did not have any authority over these camps, that they were run by the civilian authorities of Prijedor municipality." My question is: Do you stand by that statement made last July in the Stakic case?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by that. The organisation and the scheme of the camp is the work of the civilian authorities of the Prijedor municipality, of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality. And chain of command and the management, administration in the camp, was established according to what I said in my first statement, in the camps of Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje, at the main position --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I only asked you if you stood by that statement and you said that you did. I want to now refer you --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- to another issue. In your November 1994 statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you were referring -- this is on page 13 of the English version -- you were referring to the period of July, August of 1991. You said, "Retreating JNA forces at that point arrive in Prijedor. They harassed the civilian population, fired at Muslim homes," and then this is a quote directly from your statement, "The authorities had lost control and there was anarchy." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel, unfortunately, Hasan Talundic a Muslim was at the head of the police station in Prijedor who at that time and in that post was only there formally. All the Serb army units that were returning from the front in Croatia wreaked havoc in Prijedor. They would fire at random, and the security services could do nothing because they were backed by Radim Zeljaja and Vladimir Arsic and people from the military leadership in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And right after this statement: "The authorities had lost control and there was anarchy," you say the following, "The Muslim chief of police said he could do nothing as the army supported these people. I was in touch with the authorities. There was chaos in town. The police were powerless as they were mainly Serb anyway. The military effectively took over." True?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: To a certain extent, I do agree, and I said in answer to your previous question, that the police and people from the security services could do nothing because this chaos was created by drunken soldiers, soldiers who were returning from the front in Croatia, and I said that nobody could do anything with them. They were only responsible to the military leadership of the Prijedor municipality. Otherwise, there could be a confrontation because the Muslim at the head of the security service, Hasan Talundzic, it was impossible for him. These Serb soldiers running amuck throughout Prijedor were -- and they were very well armed, they were really very well armed, it was really very difficult to oppose them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this at least continued into April of 1992, because in your book, the Carsija book, you say various gangs took justice into their own hands. True? With regard to April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. But only after the takeover of power. Before the takeover, on the 30th of April, all the incidents in Prijedor were committed by members of the Serb army. Only after the takeover, on the 30th of April, which is the key date in municipality of Prijedor, then paramilitary formations and gangs began to be active in Prijedor, headed by Zoran Zigic, Djole Dosan and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Back again to your 1994 statement to the Prosecutor, page 14, and we are in the -- near the end of 1991 again, you say this: "Serbs returned from the front and the black market in weapons boomed. Automatic rifles cost a thousand Deutschmarks; semi-automatic, 800 Deutschmarks; pistols, 500 Deutschmarks; and grenades for 10 Deutschmarks. They sold in large numbers. Richer Muslims bought them." Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These were weapons that these soldiers were bringing back from the front, from the fighting in Croatia, that then were being sold to, as you say, to richer Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Amongst others. Amongst others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Amongst others, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It seems that the richer Muslims were the only buyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you answer?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Others too. Yes. Others as well, and Muslims, but Serbs didn't really need that because they received free weapons and they had large quantities of those. But in order to drink and to continue to wreak havoc in town, the Serb soldiers needed money because they didn't have too much money. They weren't really very well paid, so they needed to sell them in order to be able to continue to drink and to expand it a little. One of the main smugglers of weapons at that time was Srdjo Srdic and we mentioned him. He was a deputy in the BH assembly and later in the Serbian assembly and another person by the name of Darko Mrdja called Sula he now owns a jewellery store in Prijedor and in Belgrade, as far as I know. Srdjo Srdic and Darko Mrdja called Sula, sold weapons on behalf of the Serb Democratic Party. And all of those who bought their weapons from them later in the Omarska camp were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now about the seizure of the relay on Mount Kozara in your statement of November of 1994 which you told the judges today was the most reliable because it was closest to the events, you say that that relay was seized on 11 February, 1992, a very specific date. My first question is this: How do you know about the seizure of this relay? Where did you get the information about it? Where did you learn the details?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The date, I think, was taken by memory, but I think that it actually happened a little earlier, but let's let it stand. Simply speaking, the TV programme that we followed over that relay at the time just disappeared. Luckily for us in Prijedor, we could also receive programming over the Vlasic relay and not only over the Kozara relay, so many people turned their antennas towards the Vlasic relay. We could see that people from Yutel which is a TV agency which broadcast its programme from Sarajevo protested and said that the Kozara relay was under the control of Serbian soldiers, and that they were being prevented from transmitting or broadcasting their pictures to Bosnia, throughout Bosnia, and a large part of Croatia. I went to the Kozara relay several hundred times before that and in contacts with the editor-in-chief in Sarajevo, I was tasked with trying to go to the relay with my crew to report about what was going on there. The public didn't know who actually took control of the relay. I went to the SUP, to the security service, and together with Milos Jankovic, the man who used to be my boss and who used to be the coding and communication centre chief, and whose equipment was actually there at the relay, so together with the TV equipment. So we tried to get in touch by telephone with the crew up there, with the people who worked, the technicians who worked at the relay, who serviced the relay. However, the person who picked up the phone had a very rough voice. He said he was a captain and that his army, his military unit, had taken control of the relay, and we asked him could we come up there and tape a report about them? And they said no. More or less, he said that anybody who sets out in the direction of the relay at this time is a dead man. So we didn't later -- Serb newspapers from Banja Luka and the Serb television announced that the Kozara relay was taken over by Milinkovic. I don't know what his first name is, Milinkovic. He was a commander of a Serb paramilitary unit from the area of Prnjavor which is a town close to Banja Luka. Their war nickname was Vukovi S Vucjaka, the wolves from Vucjak, that's the Vucjak mountain. I'm trying to help the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your 1994 statement to the Prosecutor at page 17 that's exactly what you said, that the relay was seized by the wolves of Vucjak with Milinovic as their captain. I want to go back now to your statements to the German authorities and just see if you can help me understand this. What -- the statement to the German authorities says that you said this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's page 3 of the English version and document -- it's 00655982 is the ERN number at the top 25 through 30 March of 1994 is when it indicates that it was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 3 it says, "In March, 1992, I broadcast over RTV Sarajevo for the last time." Is that a true statement?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Sometime in late 1991, already our TV studio, the large TV centre in Banja Luka, through which we sent in our feed to Sarajevo, was taken over by people from the Serb Democratic Party in Banja Luka. And that studio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I hate to stop you but try to answer the question. It's a very simple question. You were being asked whether what you state in your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- is a true statement or not. Finish. That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right after that it then says that you said this: "It is correct that the transmitter in Kozara was taken over by paramilitary units (Chetniks) from Lamovita, Bisurica, and Omarska, with the support of special units in Banja Luka. This must have occurred between 21 and 28 March, 1992. Paramilitary units that did this are not the same as the so-called "Wolves." Is that what you told the German authorities?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Again, I would like to protest. The statement given to the German authorities was absolutely badly translated. It's been taken out of context. Like I said, that statement that I provided to them, I never had a chance to look at totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My only question is: Is this what you told them? Did you tell them what I just quoted to you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. I didn't say anything like that. I was decisive and specific and I said that this was committed by the wolves from Vucjak and it was done with the assistance of certain paramilitary units from the area of Lamovita and Omarska. And I insisted that they put down that this was done by the wolves from Vucjak and here it says something but that's not quite it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How is it that the German authorities got this all so wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that calls for speculation from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you know, how is it they got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, Mr. Sivac. If you can't, just say I'm not in a position to answer. If you can, answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the reasons. Probably it was a bad interpreter. Like I said, that woman had difficulty in speaking my language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you tell them that the takeover happened between 21 and 28 March, 1992? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Eight months later, after you talked to the German authorities, you then talked to the OTP, and it was that statement in which you said that it was taken over on 11 February, 1992. Where did you get that precise date from, 11 February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably I recalled that date. I located it to be on that date. But...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then I'm curious about this: You've told us that your best memory is that which is closest to the events, that being your statement of 1994. In 2001, in a telephone conversation with an OTP investigator by the name of Malik you said, "The transmitter was not taken over in February of 1992 but in the fall of 1991." My question is: What caused you in 2001, seven years later, to so dramatically change the story that you were telling in 1994?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I provided a slightly more detailed explanation at the time to Tariq Malik. The security of the Kozara relay at that time, in the autumn of 1991, was entrusted to Serbs. A Serb was in charge of the relay security. And I assume that already at that time the Kozara relay was practically in the hands of the Serbs. Later, it came out that this was actually true, when these wolves from Vucjak came to take over the relay, nobody put up any resistance, even though the people, the security people there at the relay were armed. So it was all already agreed upon. Again, I repeat, I spoke with Mr. Tariq Malik often without an interpreter, so please, all those parts of my statement that I provided to him without the presence of an interpreter, take note, because he does not speak my language very well. So please take that with some reserve. I would always object when he asked to take my statement, if I was travelling in my car or if I was at work, and I would always ask him to just do it sometimes when I was able to fully focus on that, because these events happened a long time ago, 11 years ago, so I needed time to collect myself and to recall. Sometimes I forget my date of birth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Half an hour. So may I suggest a short break of about ten minutes maximum?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because in any case, we've been sitting for an hour and a half. Ten minutes, if that's okay with you. And then we try to finish, okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a few questions now about your contention that you saw Mr. Brdjanin in Omarska, and first I want to talk a little bit about your knowledge of Mr. Brdjanin. In one of your telephone interviews with the Prosecutor, 12 December of 2001, you apparently were asked about your knowledge of Brdjanin and you said you first encountered him in 1988 or 1989. Then you said that the next time you saw him was the end of 1990 or beginning of 1991, and according to the report of that interview, you said, "I saw, end of 1990, early 1991, I saw that he was occupying a high level position in Banja Luka." Tell us what was that high level position.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you again, this stems from the interview or a conversation I had with Tariq Malik, I believe. And again, I apologise to Mr. Tariq Malik but he doesn't know my language very well, it seems to me, he speaks it poorly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your position that you did not say that? That will end it if you just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Some of it is true. Your client, Mr. Brdjanin, I met many, many years ago, perhaps he remembers that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it true that in the end of 1990 or early 1991, you saw that he was occupying a high level position in Banja Luka? Is that true or not true?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I think that this was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly at that time what his position was but in the Serb Democratic Party, he was at a high position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you say you saw that he was occupying a high level position, how did you see that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I believe it was according to newspaper articles, things that I saw in Banja Luka television, according to press clippings that I read in the Banja Luka press.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your 1994 statement to the Prosecutor at page 34 of the English version, describing the delegation visit to Omarska, you say in that statement that it happened about the 28th of July. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, around or about the 28th, in the first instance I couldn't remember the exact date. That's why I said around or about, but later on, when I linked all the events I realised that it had happened earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the linking of events you're talking about was the stories about a delegation from Banja Luka visiting Prijedor, and the newspaper article that does have a date. Is that the linking you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. A newspaper article, I saw it here for the first time, but all what I spoke about in 1994, I spoke according to my memory, to my recollection. It is possible that I have missed the date of the exact visit, that I have -- I have dated it to be, to have happened in the month of July and I stand by that. And I said about because I was not sure about the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you said "about the 28th of July," you certainly were indicating that it was near the end of July, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you again, Alma Qureshi who was the interpreter, she was interpreting the statement, and she -- I don't think that during the giving the statement I could have made so many mistakes. I think I have said about the 17th or the 18th and she had said around the 28th. Mr. Ackerman, let me tell --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You're now blaming the translator again?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Six years later I received that statement and some, many, I mean some things in that statement I don't agree with the translation, the way that it's been translated. There are problems, mistakes with the dates, and in the pronouns. I was speaking in third person singular and the lady interpreting was interpreting in the first person singular, but again this doesn't influence the crux of my statement, the essence of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you're saying that the translation from the 1994 statement is poor in many places? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Not in many places but there are mistakes and they are appearing now. Last time, in the previous trials, I have also asked for some things in that statement to be corrected, and as I said, the first time I saw the statement was six years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't they read it back to you once it was completed in 1994 and didn't you sign the bottom of every page saying that it was correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I was read the first few pages, and because the investigator stayed with me a long time, I thought that the rest of the text would not contain such major mistakes. I signed but then it turned out later that there were mistakes, mistakes in dates, mistakes in pronoun, in cases and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you missed those mistakes when it was read back to you initially? You didn't notice them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. In 1994, what was read to me was only the first few pages of my statement. As I said, because the investigators were in a hurry because another person was waiting to give a statement, so in a nonchalant way I said, I believe that you will do a good job of it and -- because I would never have said some things that are in the statement. When I was explaining to the gentleman about us Muslims, Bosniaks, I said that we, and I was speaking we, European Muslims, Bosnian Muslims, we would even drink alcohol or eat pork. And she interpreted that in the first person singular, as if I was the one who was drinking alcohol, I was the one who was eating pork. So this is just one -- one stupid mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at that statement and there is a document at the back of that statement. The first part of it is called "Witness acknowledgement." What that says is, "This statement has been read over to me in the blank language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." Then it appears to have your signature and a date. Underneath that, sir, is an interpreter's certification for Alma Qureshi. Alma Qureshi says that she has been informed that you speak and understand the Bosnian language and that she orally translated the above statement from English to the Bosnian language in the presence of Nusret Sivac who appeared to have heard and understood my translation of this statement. Nusret Sivac has acknowledged that the facts and matters set out in his statement as translated by me are true to the best of his knowledge and recollection and accordingly signed his signature where indicated. Now, I'm going to have the usher show this to you so you can tell us if that's your signature that appears on it.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said that I had signed. Yes, this is my signature, of course I said that I had signed. But as I said, only first few pages have been translated back to me. I didn't wait because it would have lasted a long time to translate everything else. And I believe that everything was fine and done correctly but here you go, there are some problems, as I can see, and last time there were too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you signed a statement saying that the entire statement had been translated to you, that was incorrect, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't incorrect. I mean I said -- I didn't -- when I signed, I didn't realise what consequences would have resulted from this. I mean, more or less. I thought that this was all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: More importantly, let's talk about Alma Qureshi who said that she read the entire statement back to you in the Bosnian language and that you said that you understood it. Now, why would she not tell the truth and sign a statement that's not the truth?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. That's her problem. And it's also my problem because I didn't understand at the time that it was that important for me to look over everything. As I said, I believed at the time I believed, I believed Ms. Qureshi who did it and the gentleman from the Tribunal. That's my fault, my -- my mistake, my error. But the essence of my statement is correct. The essence is what I have said in the statement and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You're just making this up about not having been read to you and you not having understood the mistakes in 1994 so that you can give different testimony now and make it sound plausible? Isn't that what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. No, sir, in earlier trials I said I was dissatisfied with the translation of my statement in some segments and I stand by that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you have no idea why an official interpreter would sign a false statement regarding this matter?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know, but that date, and even if I had said it, perhaps at that time, at that moment, I said it wrongly and perhaps it was wrongly translated. I don't remember. That was in 1994. That was eight, nine years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in that statement in 1994, you also said that the members of the delegation were Brdjanin, Kupresanin, and Vukic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was also incorrectly translated?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps I had said Kupresanin at the time, but I had made a mistake thinking of someone else in the delegation. I had replaced Vojo Kupresanin's name whom I knew very well and I had replaced Stojan Zupljanin's name by Vojo Kupresanin. But everything else in this statement stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So now you're saying Kupresanin was not there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you -- how about Predrag Radic? Was he there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Predrag Radic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said when this group of people arrived, that inmates from all the buildings were assembled outside, correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any exceptions to that? Was it all the inmates?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. From this northern side, I saw that almost all camp prisoners were in front of their premises on the concrete plateau, on the pista. Whether the camp prisoners from the so-called glass house were taken out, I don't know. Where the women were at the same time, again, I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After this delegation, it was a very short time, was it not, until the journalists arrived?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. Together with delegation there was also a group of reporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about -- I'm talking about the western journalists, Penny Marshall, Vulliamy, those people, they arrived --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Long, long time. These days seemed to be like eternity to us. I think these journalists arrived on the 5th of August, that's as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if this delegation you're talking about was there on 28 July, as you said initially in 1994, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I object. That misquotes, he said about the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: About the 28th of July, as you said in 1994, then the journalists who came would have come just a few days later, about a week, week to ten days. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They arrived on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then right after that, were you transferred to Trnopolje. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately, yes. There was a large group that was moved or transferred to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, before April of 2002, you made a number of statements to the OTP, to German investigators, telephone conversations with Mr. Malik. You spoke about these matters a great deal. On the 26th of April, 2002, you had a telephone conversation with Mr. Koumjian, and that was the first time that you made the assertion the delegation that visited Omarska was led by Brdjanin. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, this might be a mistake. I've never spoken on the telephone, that I recall, with Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what the document says. Let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do recall. I was in the room. There was a Suellen Taylor and I was in the room, that's correct, with an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that was the first time you made the assertion that the delegation that visited Omarska was led by Brdjanin, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you now deny your statement from 1994 where you said that Vojo Kupresanin was there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. I said that Vojo -- Brdjanin in my first statement, it was certainly said that in the delegation there was Brdjanin too. But Radic and Vojo Kupresanin too. But Vojo Kupresanin I didn't know him very well so I had replaced him with Stojan Zupljanin who was the head of the public security station at the time, and he was a member of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So now I'm confused. Is it your position that Vojo Kupresanin was there or that he was not there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. I said earlier, Mr. Ackerman, that together with Radoslav Brdjanin, Predrag Radic, Radislav Vukic, there was another person, and I know very well, and I saw that on TV, and read in the newspaper, that the main group, together with Radoslav Brdjanin, always in any political instances, there was always Vojo Kupresanin and Radislav Vukic so I had mixed up Radislav Vukic and -- sorry, I mean Vojo Kupresanin and Stojan Zupljanin because Stojan Zupljanin I didn't know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You still didn't answer my question. Is it your position that Vojo Kupresanin was there or not?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, no, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, certainly, he was not there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony in Stakic, from 30 July, at page 6.640, you said this: "At first I saw Radoslav Brdjanin with a group of collaborators who were in power, and they were the most powerful people in the so-called Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina." Who were these collaborators who you refer to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: These were Radislav Vukic, Predrag Radic, and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 6.641, 30 July, Stakic, you made this reference to Meakic. "And according to military custom, he reported to the President of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, Radoslav Brdjanin." Now, where did you get the idea that Brdjanin was president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I knew. I learned what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if it's the case that he was never the President of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection. Little relevance to the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question? I'm a little confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it's the case that he was never the President of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. He was that for sure, for certain. He was the President also of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka or Bosnian Krajina, depending all on how people referred that in writing, whether they were calling it area or a region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you are certain that he was president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and you are as certain about that as you are about everything else you've told us today, correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. When Mr. Brdjanin was in Omarska at the time, I was not clear as to his actual position, but I then saw that he had been elected precisely to be the President of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina or something like that. You see, at the time that was the Serb authorities that had created many autonomous areas, autonomous regions, whatever you want to call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you weren't clear, then please explain why you told the judges in the Stakic case, referring to Meakic, that he reported to the president of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina who was Radoslav Brdjanin, why did you tell them that if you weren't clear about whether that was true or not?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I said that at the time when he was coming to Omarska, that was what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, and you're certain of that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I am certain. I think that's what he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're as certain of that as you are about the other things you've told us today, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I read in the press, I was not present when your client was appointed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Are you as certain of that as you are of everything else you've told us today or not, just answer that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I am certain that he was at a high position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're certain -- and again I have to ask the question: As certain of that as you are about all your other testimony today? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am certain that he was at a high position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... How was this person that you believe was Brdjanin dressed in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: He was dressed in civilian clothes. I can't remember the details. I know, sir, because for a long time, I followed the visits of delegations and so on, and I know that the way that Radoslav Brdjanin was greeted and welcomed, that was only done for people who were in a very high position in authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't you say at one point that this was the only delegation that ever visited Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That was the most important political delegation that came to visit the Omarska camp. There were some other local political delegations from the Prijedor area and from the Omarska area. These were of no importance. So I don't have to mention them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't you say at one point that this was the only delegation that visited Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The most important. I think that's what I said, the most important, the most official delegations. The other delegations turned up spontaneously. They were not welcomed in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. My question is simple. Didn't you say at one point that this was the only delegation that visited Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- I think perhaps that's what I may have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to finish. We are going to have to take a little bit of time in the morning. I'm sorry, I tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Ackerman. I appreciate that. I appreciate your efforts. We'll have to conclude now, today, and unfortunately, Mr. Sivac, we need you again tomorrow morning, not for long. You will be here for a few minutes, I suppose, unless there is a long re-examination, which I don't anticipate, and after that, you can travel back home. I take it that tomorrow morning, we are -- so I suggest we start at 9.00, as planned. I suggest also that we start with the witness so that we finish with him as early as possible so that the Prosecution, or together with the other officers of the Tribunal, can start making arrangements for his flight, for his travel, and after that, we deal with the organisational matters that we have. I take it we will not be sitting in the afternoon unless there is a change in plan, because apparently there is some problem with the next witness or I don't know exactly what is happening but there is some problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could I just assure Mr. Sivac, I know he's concerned about his plans for Wednesday, that he will be leaving by at least noon tomorrow, he'll be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I anticipate Mr. Sivac that you won't be here for more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am here to do whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you all, and we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.49 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
